claim: In the mouse retina, three different types of photoreceptors provide input to 14 bipolar cell (BC) types.
source: In the mouse retina, three different types of photoreceptors provide input to 14 bipolar cell (BC) types.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, referencing established knowledge about mouse retinal organization.

claim: Most BC types are classically thought to contact all cones within their dendritic field.
source: Classically, most BC types are thought to contact all cones within their dendritic field
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is referenced in the introduction with citation to Wässle et al., 2009.

claim: ON-BCs would contact cones exclusively via invaginating synapses.
source: ON-BCs would contact cones exclusively via so-called invaginating synapses
evidence: This is stated as classical knowledge in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).

claim: OFF-BCs would form basal synapses with cones.
source: while OFF-BCs would form basal synapses
evidence: This is stated as classical knowledge in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).

claim: ON-BC type X contacted only ~20% of the cones in its dendritic field.
source: ON-BC type X contacted only ~20% of the cones in its dendritic field
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G and discussed in the Results section.

claim: ON-BC type X made mostly atypical non-invaginating contacts.
source: ON-BC type X contacted only ~20% of the cones in its dendritic field and made mostly atypical non-invaginating contacts
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4D showing that CBCX makes predominantly tip contacts rather than invaginating contacts.

claim: Types 5T, 5O and 8 contacted fewer cones than expected.
source: Types 5T, 5O and 8 also contacted fewer cones than expected.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3G showing these types contact less than 50% of cones in their dendritic field.

claim: Rod BCs received input from cones.
source: In addition, we found that rod BCs received input from cones
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5, including EM images and quantification of cone-RBC contacts.

claim: Rod and cone pathways are interconnected in both directions.
source: providing anatomical evidence that rod and cone pathways are interconnected in both directions
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing both cone-to-RBC connections (Figure 5) and rod-to-OFF-CBC connections (Figure 6).

claim: Two types of cone photoreceptors differ in their spectral properties: short (S-) and medium wavelength-sensitive (M-) cones.
source: In the mouse retina, two types of cone photoreceptors differing in their spectral properties – short (S-) and medium wavelength-sensitive (M-) cones – and rod photoreceptors provide input to 14 types of bipolar cell (reviewed in Euler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a review (Euler et al., 2014).

claim: Cone bipolar cell type 1 (CBC1) selectively contacts M-cones.
source: For example, based on electrical recordings and immunohistochemistry cone bipolar cell type 1 (CBC1) have been suggested to selectively contact M-cones, whereas CBC9 exclusively contacts S-cones (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Breuninger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous studies (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Breuninger et al., 2011).

claim: CBC9 exclusively contacts S-cones.
source: For example, based on electrical recordings and immunohistochemistry cone bipolar cell type 1 (CBC1) have been suggested to selectively contact M-cones, whereas CBC9 exclusively contacts S-cones (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Breuninger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous studies (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Breuninger et al., 2011).

claim: Other BC types are thought to contact all M-cones within their dendritic field.
source: The other BC types are thought to contact all M-cones within their dendritic field, but their connectivity to S-cones is unclear (Wässle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Wässle et al., 2009.

claim: The connectivity of other BC types to S-cones is unclear.
source: The other BC types are thought to contact all M-cones within their dendritic field, but their connectivity to S-cones is unclear (Wässle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Wässle et al., 2009.

claim: Invaginating contacts have dendritic tips extending into the cone pedicle.
source: invaginating contacts with the dendritic tips extending into the cone pedicle
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).

claim: Flat (basal) contacts touch the cone pedicle base.
source: flat (basal) contacts that touch the cone pedicle base
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).

claim: Invaginating contacts are commonly associated with ON-BCs.
source: invaginating contacts with the dendritic tips extending into the cone pedicle and flat (basal) contacts that touch the cone pedicle base, commonly associated with ON- and OFF-BCs, respectively (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).

claim: Basal contacts are commonly associated with OFF-BCs.
source: invaginating contacts with the dendritic tips extending into the cone pedicle and flat (basal) contacts that touch the cone pedicle base, commonly associated with ON- and OFF-BCs, respectively (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Kolb, 1970; Hopkins and Boycott, 1995).

claim: Rod bipolar cells (RBCs) are thought to exclusively receive rod input.
source: Rod bipolar cells (RBCs) are thought to exclusively receive rod input and to feed this signal into the cone pathway via AII amacrine cells (reviewed by Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a review (Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001).

claim: RBCs feed the rod signal into the cone pathway via AII amacrine cells.
source: Rod bipolar cells (RBCs) are thought to exclusively receive rod input and to feed this signal into the cone pathway via AII amacrine cells (reviewed by Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a review (Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001).

claim: Physiological data indicate that RBCs may receive cone photoreceptor input.
source: However, physiological data indicate that RBCs may receive cone photoreceptor input as well (Pang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Pang et al., 2010.

claim: Types CBC3A, CBC3B and CBC4 have been reported to receive direct rod input.
source: Also, types CBC3A, CBC3B and CBC4 have been reported to receive direct rod input (Mataruga et al., 2007; Haverkamp et al., 2008; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous studies (Mataruga et al., 2007; Haverkamp et al., 2008; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2014).

claim: The study analyzed an existing electron microscopy dataset (Helmstaedter et al., 2013).
source: Here, we analyzed an existing electron microscopy dataset (Helmstaedter et al., 2013) to quantify the connectivity between photoreceptors and bipolar cells in the mouse.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Helmstaedter et al., 2013.

claim: No evidence was found for additional M- or S-cone selective CBC types beyond CBC1 and CBC9.
source: We did not find evidence for additional M- or S-cone selective CBC types in addition to the reported CBC1 and 9.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from the analysis of the EM dataset.

claim: CBCX is likely an ON-CBC.
source: The newly discovered CBCX (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), likely an ON-CBC (Ichinose et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Helmstaedter et al., 2013 and Ichinose et al., 2014.

claim: The study used the serial block-face electron microscopy (SBEM) dataset e2006 published by Helmstaedter et al. (2013).
source: We used the serial block-face electron microscopy (SBEM) dataset e2006 published by Helmstaedter et al. (2013) to analyze the connectivity between photoreceptors and bipolar cells in the outer plexiform layer (OPL) of the mouse retina (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Helmstaedter et al., 2013.

claim: 163 cone axon terminals (cone pedicles) were reconstructed in the dataset.
source: To this end, we reconstructed the volume of all cone axon terminals (cone pedicles; n = 163) in the dataset
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the reconstruction work.

claim: 451 bipolar cell dendritic trees were reconstructed in the dataset.
source: as well as the dendritic trees of all BCs (n = 451; Figure 1B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the reconstruction work.

claim: Type nine cone bipolar cells selectively target S-cones.
source: To identify S- and M-cones, we used the fact that type nine cone bipolar cells selectively target S-cones (Figure 1C,D) (Mariani, 1984; Kouyama and Marshak, 1992; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Breuninger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies (Mariani, 1984; Kouyama and Marshak, 1992; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Breuninger et al., 2011).

claim: 48 contacts of CBC9s and cones were found.
source: We found 48 contacts of CBC9s and cones, involving 43 cones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: 29 of the CBC9-cone contacts were in the periphery of the cone pedicle where no synapses are expected.
source: We visually assessed all contacts and found that 29 of these were in the periphery of the cone pedicle, where no synapses are expected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Chun et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies (Dowling and Boycott, 1966; Chun et al., 1996).

claim: 14 potential S-cones had invaginating contacts from at least one CBC9.
source: This left 14 potential S-cones with invaginating contacts from at least one CBC9.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the S-cone identification process.

claim: S-cones are contacted by the dendrites of all neighboring CBC9s.
source: It has been shown that S-cones are contacted by the dendrites of all neighboring CBC9s and that these contacts occur mostly at the tip of dendritic branches (Haverkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Haverkamp et al., 2005.

claim: CBC9 contacts to S-cones occur mostly at the tip of dendritic branches.
source: It has been shown that S-cones are contacted by the dendrites of all neighboring CBC9s and that these contacts occur mostly at the tip of dendritic branches (Haverkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Haverkamp et al., 2005.

claim: Six cones were defined as S-cones based on having at least two invaginating contacts from CBC9s.
source: The other six cones had at least two invaginating contacts from CBC9s. These originated from two different CBC9s or – in case they originated only from a single CBC9 – at least one of them was formed by a dendritic branch ending at the cone (Figure 1E). We labeled the eight cones that featured only a single CBC9 contact as M-cones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and defined the remaining six candidate cones as S-cones
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the S-cone identification criteria.

claim: The identified S-cone fraction was 4.8% (6/124 cones).
source: This corresponds to a fraction of 4.8% S-cones (6/124 cones within the dendritic field of at least one CBC9), matching the 3–5% reported in previous studies (Röhlich et al., 1994; Haverkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies (Röhlich et al., 1994; Haverkamp et al., 2005).

claim: Previous studies reported 3-5% S-cones.
source: This corresponds to a fraction of 4.8% S-cones (6/124 cones within the dendritic field of at least one CBC9), matching the 3–5% reported in previous studies (Röhlich et al., 1994; Haverkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies (Röhlich et al., 1994; Haverkamp et al., 2005).

claim: An alternative classification scheme would have resulted in 14 S-cones out of 124 cones (11.3%).
source: An alternative scheme for identifying S-cones would have been to classify all cones with at least one invaginating contact from CBC9 as S-cones. This would have resulted in a total of 14 S-cones out of 124 cones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) or a fraction of 11.3%.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing an alternative analysis.

claim: The alternative S-cone classification of 11.3% is much larger than the 3-5% reported earlier and is considered very unlikely (p=0.0037).
source: Because this S-cone percentage is much larger than the 3–5% reported earlier (Haverkamp et al., 2005), we consider this scenario as very unlikely (p=0.0037, binomial test, null hypothesis: 5% S-cones, n = 124).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a statistical test and citation to Haverkamp et al., 2005.

claim: The tissue in the dataset was stained to enhance cell-surface contrast to enable automatic reconstruction.
source: As the tissue in the dataset was stained to enhance cell-surface contrast to enable automatic reconstruction, it is not possible to distinguish between synaptic contacts based on explicit ultrastructural synaptic markers, such as vesicles, synaptic ribbons or postsynaptic densities (see also discussion in Helmstaedter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Helmstaedter et al., 2013.

claim: It is not possible to distinguish between synaptic contacts in the dataset based on explicit ultrastructural synaptic markers.
source: As the tissue in the dataset was stained to enhance cell-surface contrast to enable automatic reconstruction, it is not possible to distinguish between synaptic contacts based on explicit ultrastructural synaptic markers, such as vesicles, synaptic ribbons or postsynaptic densities (see also discussion in Helmstaedter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Helmstaedter et al., 2013.

claim: The highly stereotypical morphology of synapses at photoreceptor axon terminals allowed classification of contacts.
source: In contrast to the synaptic contacts in the inner plexiform layer studied by Helmstaedter et al. (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), the highly stereotypical morphology of synapses at photoreceptor axon terminals allowed us to classify the contacts (Haverkamp et al., 2000)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Helmstaedter et al., 2013 and Haverkamp et al., 2000.

claim: Ribbon synapses of cones are placed exclusively in the presynaptic area at the bottom of the cone pedicles.
source: The ribbon synapses of the cones are placed exclusively in the presynaptic area at the bottom of the cone pedicles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the anatomy of cone synapses.

claim: ON-cone bipolar cells make invaginating contacts where the dendritic tips reach a few hundred nanometers into the presynaptic area of cone pedicles.
source: Here, ON-cone bipolar cells (ON-CBCs) make invaginating contacts, where the dendritic tips reach a few hundred nanometers into the presynaptic area of cone pedicles (Figure 2A) (Dowling and Boycott, 1966).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Dowling and Boycott, 1966.

claim: OFF-cone BCs make basal contacts in the presynaptic area of cone pedicles.
source: In contrast, OFF-cone BCs (OFF-CBCs) make basal contacts in the same area (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the anatomy of OFF-CBC contacts.

claim: A total of 20,944 contacts were found in 2,620 pairs of cones and BCs.
source: In total, we found n = 20,944 contacts in n = 2620 pairs of cones and BCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the contact detection.

claim: A support vector machine (SVM) classifier was trained to distinguish whether or not an individual BC obtains input from a cone.
source: We trained a support vector machine (SVM) classifier to distinguish whether or not an individual BC obtains input from a cone (as opposed to classifying each individual contact site, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the classification method.

claim: Seven features were defined for contact classification, including contact area, eccentricity and contact height.
source: To this end, we defined a set of seven features, including contact area, eccentricity and contact height, which allowed distinguishing between potential synaptic contacts and 'false' contacts (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures showing the features.

claim: A randomly selected set of contacts was manually labeled for training (n = 50 for OFF-CBCs, n = 108 for ON-CBCs and n = 67 for RBCs).
source: For training of the classifier, we manually labeled a randomly selected set of contacts (n = 50 for OFF-CBCs, n = 108 for ON-CBCs and n = 67 for RBCs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the training data.

claim: Separate classifiers were trained for ON-CBCs, OFF-CBCs and RBCs.
source: We trained separate classifiers for ON-CBCs, OFF-CBCs and RBCs
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the classification approach.

claim: The classifiers could reliably distinguish between true and false contacts with a success rate of ~90%.
source: and found that they could reliably distinguish between true and false contacts, with a success rate of ~90% (leave-one-out cross-validation accuracy, Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to figures showing the classification performance.

claim: Deviations between automatic classifier and human labels did not vary systematically with BC type.
source: Deviations between the labels of the automatic classifier and the human labels did not vary systematically with BC type (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the classification performance.

claim: Type 5 CBCs were classified into three types in agreement with recent reports.
source: To this end, we classified type 5 CBCs, which had not been further subdivided by Helmstaedter et al. (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), into three types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods) in agreement with recent reports (Greene et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Helmstaedter et al., 2013 and Greene et al., 2016.

claim: S-cones and M-cones contacted 12.2 ± 1.5 CBCs (n = 5 cones) and 12.2 ± 0.4 CBCs (n = 71 cones), respectively.
source: There was no difference in the number of CBCs contacted by S- and M-cones with 12.2 ± 1.5 CBCs (n = 5 cones, mean ± SEM) for S-cones and 12.2 ± 0.4 CBCs (n = 71 cones) for M-cones, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with quantitative data.

claim: The total number of contact points per cone was almost identical for S- and M-cones with an average of 108 ± 24 per S-cone and 105 ± 5 per M-cone.
source: Similarly, the total number of contact points per cone was almost identical for S- and M-cones with an average of 108 ± 24 per S- and 105 ± 5 per M-cone.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with quantitative data.

claim: Most CBC types were contacted predominantly by M-cones, with an average of 2-6 cones contacting individual CBCs.
source: Most CBC types were contacted predominantly by M-cones, with an average of 2–6 cones contacting individual CBCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3B showing the data.

claim: CBC9 received considerable S-cone input.
source: One exception was the CBC9 that – by our definition of S-cones – received considerable S-cone input.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3B showing the data.

claim: A few contacts were detected between CBC9s and M-cones.
source: We also detected a few contacts between CBC9s and M-cones; these are a consequence of our restrictive definition of S-cone and originate from those cones for which we found only single CBC9 contacts, such that they were classified as M-cone
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the CBC9-M-cone contacts.

claim: Each M-cone contacted on average a little less than one CBC1.
source: We found that each M-cone contacted on average a little less than one CBC1, while S-cones contacted almost no CBC1, consistent with previous reports (Breuninger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Breuninger et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: S-cones contacted almost no CBC1, consistent with previous reports.
source: We found that each M-cone contacted on average a little less than one CBC1, while S-cones contacted almost no CBC1, consistent with previous reports (Breuninger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Breuninger et al., 2011 and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: M-cones almost never contacted CBC9s.
source: Conversely, we found that M-cones almost never contacted CBC9s (see above), but S-cones contacted on average two.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: S-cones contacted on average two CBC9s.
source: Conversely, we found that M-cones almost never contacted CBC9s (see above), but S-cones contacted on average two.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Both S- and M-cone types contacted all other CBC types.
source: Both cone types contacted all other CBC types (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Each cone made contact with at least one CBC2, 3B, 4, 5I, 6 and 7.
source: with each cone making contact with at least one CBC2, 3B, 4, 5I, 6 and 7.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Some cones did not contact ON-CBC types 5T, 5O, X and 8.
source: In contrast, some cones did not contact ON-CBC types 5T, 5O, X and 8, such that they were contacted by considerably less than one cone on average.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: OFF-CBCs (types 1-4) contacted on average 65-75% of the cones in their dendritic field.
source: OFF-CBCs (types 1–4) contacted on average 65–75% of the cones in their dendritic field, with very similar numbers across types (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3G showing the data.

claim: ON-CBC types 5I, 6 and 7 contacted 60-80% of cones within their dendritic field.
source: The connectivity pattern of types 5I, 6 and 7 was similar to that observed in the OFF types (Figure 3G); these cells sampled from the majority of cones within their dendritic field (60–80%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3G showing the data.

claim: CBC5T, 5O, X and 8 contacted less than half of the cones within their dendritic field.
source: CBC5T, 5O, X and 8, however, contacted less than half of the cones within their dendritic field (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3G showing the data.

claim: CBCX contacted the lowest fraction of cones (~20%) within its dendritic field.
source: with the lowest fraction contacted by CBCX (~20%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3G showing the data.

claim: Dendrites of CBC5T, 5O, X and 8 were frequently found passing underneath a cone with a distance of 1-3 µm without contacting it.
source: This result is not due to a systematic error in our contact classification: We manually checked volume-reconstructed dendritic trees of the respective types for completeness and frequently found dendrites passing underneath a cone with a distance of 1–3 µm without contacting it (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a supplementary figure showing examples.

claim: Almost all CBC types received input at a very similar location relative to their soma.
source: Almost all CBC types received input at a very similar location relative to their soma, except for CBCX
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3H and I showing the contact density analysis.

claim: CBCX received the majority of inputs closer to the soma than all other types relative to its dendritic field size.
source: except for CBCX, which received the majority of inputs closer to the soma than all other types relative to its dendritic field size.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3I showing the normalized contact density.

claim: CBCX has a compact dendritic tree.
source: This BC type has only recently been identified by (Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Shekhar et al., 2016). It has a compact dendritic tree
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Helmstaedter et al., 2013 and Shekhar et al., 2016.

claim: CBCX has a relatively wide axonal terminal system.
source: but a relatively wide axonal terminal system
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing CBCX morphology.

claim: CBCX axonal terminal stratifies narrowly at approximately the same depth as CBC5O and 5I.
source: that stratifies narrowly at approximately the same depth as CBC5O and 5I do.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing CBCX morphology.

claim: CBCX samples cone input very sparsely, with input from only two cones on average.
source: Interestingly, CBCX seems to sample the cone input very sparsely, with input from only two cones on average
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C,D showing the data.

claim: Dendrites of CBCX oftentimes passed underneath cones or stopped shortly before cone pedicles without making contacts.
source: In fact, dendrites of CBCX oftentimes passed underneath cones or even stopped shortly before cone pedicles without making contacts at all (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4A and B showing examples.

claim: All CBCX skeletons were independently verified and corrected where necessary.
source: It is unlikely that this resulted from incomplete skeletons for these BCs, as all skeletons were independently verified for this study and corrected where necessary (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing quality control.

claim: Very few CBCX-cone contacts were 'classical' invaginating ON-CBC contacts (3 out of 19 contacts, n = 7 cells).
source: We re-examined all detected contacts between CBCXs and cones and found that very few of those were 'classical' invaginating ON-CBC contacts (3 out of 19 contacts, n = 7 cells, Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4B-D showing the data.

claim: The vast majority of CBCX-cone contacts were 'tip' contacts (16 out of 19 contacts, n = 7 cells).
source: The vast majority were 'tip' contacts (16 out of 19 contacts, n = 7 cells), which were similar to basal contacts made by OFF-CBC dendrites (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4B-D showing the data.

claim: CBCX tip contacts were similar to basal contacts made by OFF-CBC dendrites.
source: The vast majority were 'tip' contacts (16 out of 19 contacts, n = 7 cells), which were similar to basal contacts made by OFF-CBC dendrites (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4B-D showing the data.

claim: The available data was not conclusive regarding whether CBCX tip contacts are smaller than those of OFF-CBCs.
source: The available data was not conclusive with regards to the question whether these tip contacts of CBCX are smaller than those of OFF-CBCs (median area: 0.05 µm2 for n = 22 CBCX contacts; 0.10 µm2 for n = 23 OFF-CBC contacts, but p=0.17, Wilcoxon ranksum test).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis.

claim: Other ON-CBC types made mostly invaginating contacts (71 out of 81 contacts, n = 12 cells).
source: In contrast to the CBCX, the other ON-CBC types made mostly invaginating contacts (71 out of 81 contacts, n = 12 cells, two cells per BC type, Figure 4D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4D showing the data.

claim: There is a significant effect of cell type on contact type (GLM with Poisson output distribution, n = 38, interaction: p=3.6x10−7).
source: indicating a significant effect of cell type on contact type (GLM with Poisson output distribution, n = 38, interaction: p=3.6x10−7, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis.

claim: CBCX did not receive any rod input.
source: We checked if CBCX receive rod input instead but did not observe any rod contacts (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of CBCX contacts.

claim: CBCX is most likely an ON-CBC based on axonal stratification depth and recent electrophysiological and functional recordings.
source: Still, based on the axonal stratification depth (Helmstaedter et al., 2013) and recent electrophysiological and functional recordings (Ichinose et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2016) this BC type is most likely an ON-CBC, supported by its mGluR6 expression (Shekhar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies (Helmstaedter et al., 2013; Ichinose et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2016; Shekhar et al., 2016).

claim: CBCX expresses mGluR6.
source: supported by its mGluR6 expression (Shekhar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Shekhar et al., 2016.

claim: Three cells labeled as RBC in Helmstaedter et al. (2013) were excluded from the RBC analysis because they did not contact any rods.
source: Three cells labeled as RBC in Helmstaedter et al. (Helmstaedter et al., 2013) were excluded from this analysis, as they did not contact any rods (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Some rods were not contacted by any RBC, likely due to incomplete tracing of fine dendritic tips of some RBCs.
source: We also found some rods not contacted by any RBC, which is likely due to incomplete tracing of the fine dendritic tips of some RBCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining missing rod-RBC contacts.

claim: RBCs contacted both rod spherules and cone pedicles.
source: In fact, RBCs did not only contact rod spherules but also cone pedicles (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5A,B showing the data.

claim: RBC-cone contacts were typical ON-CBC contacts with invaginating dendritic tips into the cone pedicles.
source: These contacts were typical ON-CBC contacts with invaginating dendritic tips into the cone pedicles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5B showing EM images.

claim: 75% of RBCs contacted at least one cone.
source: While the vast majority (75%) contacted at least one cone, only 25% of all RBCs (n = 141) did not contact any (Figure 5C).

claim: CBC5s were classified into three subtypes based on axonal density profiles using principal component analysis and Gaussian mixture model fitting.

(Greene et al., 2016): First, we calculated the densities of both ON- and OFF-starburst amacrine cells (SACs) dendrites along the optical axis. We fitted the peak of these profiles with a surface using bivariate B-splines of third order. Next, we corrected the density profiles of CBC5 axonal trees by mapping the SAC surfaces to parallel planes. We then applied principal component analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) to obtain a first clustering into three groups by fitting a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) (Bishop, 2006) with three components onto the first three principal components of the axon density profiles.

claim: The model yielded a significant intercept (z = 8.72, p<0.0001), a significant main effect of cell type (z = 4.11, p=4x10−4), a significant main effect of contact type (z = 2.66, p=0.008) and a significant interaction cell x contact type (z = −5.09, p<3.6x10−7).
